strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: The Cauchy factorization of the GFT (Theorem 3.1) is original, rigorously proven, and generalizes prior work to arbitrary hierarchical graphs. Treatment of edge cases (repeated eigenvalues, orthogonal updates) is careful and thorough.

Rigorous algorithmic design and analysis: Theorem 3.2 provides formal O(n²k) complexity characterization with clear dependence on interface size. Greedy HGF construction and interface sparsification with theoretical guarantees (Theorem 4.1) demonstrate thoughtful algorithm engineering.

Compelling synthetic validation: Figures 2-3 convincingly demonstrate predicted O(n²k) and O(k) scaling laws, with negligible preprocessing overhead. Theory-practice alignment on controlled synthetic graphs is excellent.

Parameter efficiency and interpretability: Achieves competitive performance with orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters than transformer baselines. Grad-CAM analysis (Figure 5) provides intuitive evidence of localized spectral processing.
Strong mathematical exposition: Comprehensive proofs, careful notation, effective use of appendices. Core theoretical ideas are clearly motivated and well-developed.
weaknesses: Marginal empirical improvements with large error bars: Real-world performance gains over Stable-ChebNet are within or overlap standard deviations on 3/4 datasets (Roman-Empire: 92.12±1.12 vs 92.03±0.85; Amazon-Ratings: 53.41±1.3 vs 53.15±0.2; Tolokers: 85.57±0.61 vs 85.55±3.34). Only Minesweeper shows clear improvement. With only 4 datasets from a single benchmark, practical impact is unclear.

Critical theory-practice gap on complexity: Quadratic complexity O(n²k) requires small interface size k=O(1). For general graphs, k can be O(n), reverting to O(n³). Tolokers—explicitly called a 'worst-case scenario'—has k=25 after aggressive sparsification, yet is presented as a success. No characterization of when favorable hierarchical structure occurs in practice.

Unquantified approximation error propagation: Theorem 4.1 guarantees (1±ε)-spectral equivalence but ε is never specified for tested datasets. The claim that O(ε·L)-bounded output deviation holds for Lipschitz filters appears after Theorem 4.1 without empirical validation. Impact of 99.5% edge sparsification on spectral properties not studied. No ablation on sparsification ratio.

Extensive dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning without principled guidance: Table 3 reveals dramatic variation (Layers: 3-14, K: 4-8, Banks vary, Dropout: 0.2-0.3, Sparsification: 0.005-0.01). No ablation studies justifying these choices. No clear procedure for practitioners to set hyperparameters on new datasets. Unclear whether improvements stem from method or careful tuning.

Limited experimental scope: Only 4 datasets from single benchmark (Platonov et al., 2023). All transductive despite claiming inductive compatibility—no inductive experiments. Graphs are small (10K-24K nodes); no large-scale experiments where O(n²) savings would be most impactful. Missing comparisons with other spectral methods beyond Stable-ChebNet and Global GFT.

Incremental architectural contribution: Section 5 applies the factorization straightforwardly with standard learnable filters. ODE-inspired formulation (Eq. 18-19) relegated to appendix and feels disconnected. No ablation studies on number of hierarchy levels L, number of filter banks, or filter parameterization choices. Why this specific architecture?

Unsubstantiated theoretical claims: Connection between spectral locality (Definition A, appendix) and practical node-domain locality not rigorously established. Claims about avoiding oversquashing lack formal justification. Figure 5's localization interpretation is suggestive but not rigorous.

Presentation and reproducibility gaps: Important details scattered across appendices (ODE formulation B.1, learnable filters B.2, deflation C). Unclear when to use L2G-Net versus alternatives—only vague guidance ('when long-range dependencies essential'). No discussion of failure modes. Inconsistent use of normalized vs. combinatorial Laplacian. No code provided.

strengths: Novel Cauchy factorization framework: The exact factorization of the GFT via Cauchy matrices (Theorem 3.1) is mathematically elegant and original, with rigorous proofs and careful treatment of edge cases (repeated eigenvalues, deflation)
Validated theoretical complexity: Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 provide clear complexity bounds; synthetic experiments (Figures 2-3) convincingly validate O(kn²) scaling prediction with controlled structure
Thoughtful algorithmic design: Greedy HGF construction minimizing factorization cost, spectral sparsification with guarantees, and complete handling of numerical cases show maturity
Parameter efficiency: Achieves competitive performance with orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters than attention-based baselines (Figure 4), providing practical advantage
Rigorous mathematical treatment: Comprehensive proofs in appendix, careful handling of notation, treatment of subtle cases (repeated eigenvalues, deflation, affected spectral indices)
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Method's theoretical O(kn²) advantage assumes hierarchical graphs with small interfaces, but experiments apply to general heterophilous graphs without measuring hierarchical structure; Tolokers explicitly noted as worst-case with k=25 providing minimal speedup (91.3s vs 117.6s)

Marginal empirical improvements: Table 1 shows L2G-Net loses on 3 of 4 datasets vs Polynormer (Roman-Empire: 92.12 vs 92.55; Amazon: 53.41 vs 54.81; Tolokers: 85.57 vs 85.91), with only 0.04% gain on Minesweeper—insufficient justification for methodological complexity

Incomplete computational cost analysis: Table 2 omits preprocessing time (partition finding via spectral bisection + sparsification); Theorem 4.1 shows sparsification can increase interface size to O(n log n/ε²), potentially negating theoretical advantages—this trade-off never discussed

Missing critical experiments and ablations: No experiments on graphs with true hierarchical structure (where method should excel); no systematic studies of partition quality effects, hierarchy depth L, or sparsification ratio; no identification of graph properties making method effective; no guidance on when practitioners should use L2G-Net

Limited architectural novelty: The GNN design (Section 5, Eq. 10) is straightforward—learnable filters + Cauchy factors + hierarchical composition. This natural instantiation adds little beyond the factorization itself; why this particular design improves performance is unexplained

Experimental scope limitations: Only one benchmark suite (Platonov et al. 2023); transductive setting only; no experiments on standard benchmarks (OGB, Planetoid) or natural hierarchical graphs (protein networks, hierarchical clustering); results don't demonstrate generalizability

Presentation gaps: Missing intuition for why Cauchy factors are the right decomposition; Figure 1 is unclear about what happens at each hierarchical level; paper lacks guidance on when to use L2G-Net vs alternatives; notation-heavy introduction without motivation

Unaccounted numerical and practical issues: Numerical stability of secular equation solving with repeated eigenvalues not thoroughly discussed; sensitivity to Laplacian type (normalized vs combinatorial) unexplored; weighted graphs assumed but not studied; total end-to-end time including preprocessing never compared

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: Theorem 3.1 elegantly generalizes Cauchy factorization from path graphs to arbitrary hierarchical graph families; Theorem 3.2 establishes clear O(n²k) complexity with thorough proofs
Synthetic experiments convincingly validate theoretical predictions: Figures 2-3 demonstrate predicted O(kn²) scaling and O(k) linear scaling with interface size, confirming theory-practice alignment
Well-motivated problem articulation: Clear identification of fundamental trade-off between global spectral methods (expensive O(n³)) and local message-passing (efficient but limited receptive field)

Rigorous mathematical treatment: Careful handling of edge cases including repeated eigenvalues via deflation (Section C), spectral sparsification with formal guarantees (Theorem 4.1), and detailed algorithmic descriptions
Interpretability analysis demonstrates principled locality-globality trade-off: Grad-CAM study (Figure 5) shows L2G-Net concentrates attributions on smaller node subsets compared to fully global GFT
weaknesses: Limited empirical superiority on real-world benchmarks: Underperforms state-of-the-art on 3/4 test datasets (Roman-Empire: 92.12 vs Polynormer 92.55; Amazon-Ratings: 53.41 vs 54.81; Tolokers: 85.57 vs 85.91)

Modest practical speedups limited to preprocessing: Table 2 shows only 2-3× speedup on preprocessing while eigendecomposition is computed once; no end-to-end training time comparisons provided, limiting practical impact

Questionable alignment with real-world graph properties: Benchmarks designed for non-local dependencies not necessarily hierarchical structure; aggressive sparsification required (k=25 vs original degree 88), suggesting artificial hierarchy

Specialized applicability significantly limits scope: Method efficiency critically depends on finding hierarchical decompositions with small interface sizes; applicability unclear for graphs without natural modular structure; no evaluation on graphs with strong hierarchical properties

Limited experimental scope: Single benchmark suite with 4 datasets; missing comparisons with other fast spectral methods (Givens rotations, butterfly factorizations); no ablations on sparsification ratio impact

Unclear when to adopt over alternatives: Paper acknowledges specialization to hierarchical structures but provides limited guidance on detecting/exploiting such structure; no analysis of what fraction of real-world graphs benefit

Hyperparameter sensitivity not addressed: Table 3 shows large variance in dataset-specific settings (layers: 3-14, filter banks: 1-6, sparsification: 0.005-0.01); hyperparameter selection process not explained
Theoretical limitations underexplored: Conditions for efficiency (small k) not formally characterized for real graphs; worst-case complexity remains O(n³) when k→O(n)

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: Rigorous generalization of Cauchy factorization from path graphs to arbitrary symmetric matrices, with sound complexity analysis (O(kn²)) validated experimentally on synthetic graphs
Novel architecture design: L2G-Net's principle of inserting learnable filters between hierarchical Cauchy factors represents a genuine contribution combining local and global spectral processing

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Covers synthetic validation, transductive heterophilous benchmarks, inductive long-range tasks, and large-scale graphs (569k nodes); demonstrates scalability where full eigendecomposition fails
Parameter efficiency: Orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters than transformer baselines (Figure 5) while maintaining competitive accuracy—a meaningful practical advantage
Thorough presentation: Extensive supplementary materials with complete proofs, detailed algorithms, and careful treatment of edge cases (deflation, near-degenerate eigenvalues)
Interpretability: Learned filters show task-adaptive frequency responses (Figure 9) and node-level attribution is more localized than global spectral or attention methods (Figure 6)
weaknesses: Limited practical speedup: Per-epoch cost is O(n²), making L2G-Net 2-20× slower than GCN/ChebNet (Table 11); wall-clock advantage only from faster convergence, not algorithmic efficiency (Table 10)

Inconsistent and modest empirical results: Often competitive but rarely clearly superior—Minesweeper within std dev of Polynormer (97.50 vs 97.46), Roman-empire lags (92.12 vs 92.55); performance improvements frequently within error margins

Narrow target regime with unclear applicability: Method requires hierarchical graph structure (k ≪ n) and preference for spectral processing; paper does not characterize what fraction of real-world graphs satisfy these conditions or provide guidance on when to use L2G-Net vs. alternatives

Missing critical ablations: No analysis of sensitivity to hierarchy depth L, sparsification ratio ρ, or comparison of greedy partitioning to alternative methods (METIS, recursive bisection); design choices in Table 8 appear arbitrary without justification

Unanalyzed approximation error propagation: Spectral sparsification introduces error ε (Theorem 4.1), but empirical impact on GNN performance across multiple layers is not validated; theoretical guarantees and practical degradation may diverge
Partition quality heuristic without guarantees: Greedy HGF construction lacks optimality guarantees; no comparison to optimal or alternative partitions for the same graphs
Large error bars in results: Several benchmarks (Table 2 Roman-empire: ±1.1%, Table 7 London: 55.6±0.6) have overlapping confidence intervals, weakening conclusions about superiority
Limited benchmark diversity: Focuses on heterophilous and long-range regimes (specialized); omits standard homophilic benchmarks (Cora, Citeseer, OGB), limiting assessment of general applicability

strengths: Novel exact Cauchy factorization of the GFT (Theorem 3.1) with rigorous mathematical proofs and generalization from prior path-graph results to arbitrary symmetric matrices
Solid theoretical complexity analysis validated by synthetic experiments; O(kn²) scaling confirmed empirically across graph sizes (Figures 3-4)
Comprehensive evaluation across heterophilous benchmarks, long-range molecular graphs, and large-scale city networks (up to 569k nodes)
Significant parameter efficiency: achieves competitive accuracy with orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters than transformer baselines
Honest treatment of limitations; authors acknowledge method is unsuitable for linear-complexity-critical settings and provide thorough related work discussion (Appendix B)
Interpretability analysis (Grad-CAM, learned filter visualizations) demonstrates local-to-global spectral processing with clear locality properties
Thorough treatment of technical edge cases including deflation for degenerate eigenvalues and spectral sparsification guarantees (Theorem 4.1)
weaknesses: Marginal and inconsistent accuracy results: L2G-Net performs worse than or tied with baselines on most benchmarks (Roman-empire: 92.12% vs Polynormer 92.55%; Amazon-ratings: 53.39% vs 54.81%; LRGB peptides-func: 72.14 vs S2GCN 72.75); claimed 'competitive' results are misleading when never exceeding SOTA

High per-epoch computational cost (0.35–1.54 s/epoch) despite theoretical speedups—3–20× slower than ChebNet/GCN per epoch; end-to-end competitive times rely on fewer convergence epochs, which is not theoretically guaranteed and dataset-dependent

Sparsification introduces unquantified error: while Theorem 4.1 bounds spectral error, the impact on task performance depends on Lipschitz constants never computed; no ablations isolate sparsification error or show accuracy-speedup tradeoff

Graph-specific architecture limits generalizability: partitions are recomputed per graph in inductive settings, introducing unaccounted latency; inductive experiments (Section 6.3) ignore train-test distribution shift and never validate transfer learning

Missing mechanistic understanding: no ablations on hierarchy depth (L=1 vs L=4), partition quality, or worst-case analysis of graphs with large cuts; unclear when the method provides advantages over simpler spectral approaches
Greedy partition algorithm lacks theoretical guarantees: Section 4.1 uses heuristic spectral bisection with no approximation bounds; condition (7) is applied greedily without proof of near-optimality

Limited neural network innovation: once the Cauchy factorization exists, the L2G-Net architecture (Eq. 10) follows straightforwardly; architectural novelty beyond 'insert learnable filters between factors' is minimal

Missing comparisons to approximate spectral methods: no evaluation against randomized SVD, Lanczos-based eigensolvers, or other O(n² log n) approximate spectral approaches that might compete with the O(kn²) method

Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned; Table 8 shows high hyperparameter sensitivity (sparsification 0.005–0.150 across datasets) requiring non-trivial tuning; implementation details sparse (numerical stability, Cauchy matrix storage)

Weak expressiveness result (Theorem 5.1): while showing L2G-Net strictly contains global spectral filters, the practical significance is unclear given Cayley-Hamilton implies any finite-graph function is expressible; doesn't characterize which functions benefit from partition structure

Deflation treatment feels ad-hoc: near-degenerate eigenvalues are handled post-hoc in Appendix D rather than integrated into main theory; practical impact on complexity and stability not fully characterized
Incomplete sparsification evaluation: no experiments varying ε to isolate accuracy loss; Table 3 shows minimal speedup (1.3×) on dense graphs (Tolokers, k=25) with unknown accuracy cost

strengths: Novel Cauchy factorization theorem that generalizes prior work from path graphs to arbitrary graphs, enabling exact hierarchical decomposition of the GFT with O(kn²) complexity rather than O(n³)

Strong theoretical contributions with rigorous proofs handling repeated eigenvalues and non-orthogonal updates through deflation, plus expressiveness result (Theorem 5.1) proving strict containment over global spectral filters
Scalability breakthrough enabling spectral processing on previously infeasible large graphs (569k nodes in 144 minutes vs. projected 23+ days), demonstrated via comprehensive synthetic validation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four distinct benchmark suites (heterophilous, long-range inductive/transductive, molecular) with proper statistical reporting and honest comparisons
Significant parameter efficiency: competitive accuracy with orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters than state-of-the-art transformer baselines (e.g., Table 5)
Well-executed presentation with clear motivation, effective visualizations (Figures 1-2), and extensive appendices providing detailed proofs, algorithms, and implementation details
Honest limitations discussion appropriately identifying when the method is/isn't suitable, enhancing credibility and guiding practitioners
Strong reproducibility: detailed algorithms, hyperparameter tables, dataset specifications, and implementation guidance enable reproduction
weaknesses: Empirical performance improvements are sometimes modest and within noise margins on key benchmarks (e.g., Roman-empire: 92.12 vs 92.55; Amazon-ratings: 53.39 vs 54.81), limiting practical significance in some settings
Substantial per-epoch computational overhead compared to simpler methods (Table 11: 1.54s/epoch on Roman-empire vs 0.40s for ChebNet), though mitigated by faster convergence in end-to-end training

Method effectiveness depends critically on finding partitions with small cuts; for graphs without hierarchical structure, greedy bisection may yield poor partitions with limited guidance on when the approach will succeed

Sparsification introduces approximation error with only high-level spectral guarantees (Theorem 4.1); empirical quantification of how approximation impacts downstream accuracy across different graph types is lacking
Limited architectural novelty in L2G-Net design itself (Eq. 10)—straightforward local filtering + Cauchy multiplication; primary novelty is in enabling this structure rather than the architecture
Results on some benchmarks show underperformance relative to baselines with positional encodings (e.g., peptides-func: L2G-Net+PE achieves 72.46 vs S2GCN+PE 73.11), with limited analysis of why

Scope is somewhat specialized (hierarchical graphs with long-range dependencies) rather than broadly applicable; unclear decision-making guidance for practitioners on when L2G-Net is preferable to alternatives
Hyperparameter tuning complexity introduced by sparsification (Table 8 shows dataset-specific ratios ranging from 0.005 to 1.0) without principled guidelines for selection
